analysis.one_liner: Lets states, local governments, tribes, and private parties take over endangered species management, and exempts those deals from environmental review.
analysis.headline: Rep. Don Young's bill to shift endangered species management to states and local parties gathered 8 Republican cosponsors but never left the House Natural Resources Committee, dying when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite a core section of the Endangered Species Act. It would let the Interior and Commerce Departments sign management agreements not just with states but with local governments, Indian tribes, and private parties, and hand over species management entirely to states that run an 'adequate' conservation program, with the federal government covering up to 90% of the cost. Deals struck under the bill would be exempt from National Environmental Policy Act review, and parties to a deal could not face new restrictions, payments, or mitigation requirements later. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Natural Resources Committee and its wildlife subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners, developers, and resource industries facing endangered species restrictions would gain the most: agreements lock in their obligations ('no surprises'), shield agreement activities from the ESA's land-acquisition, consultation, and takings prohibitions, and bar new restrictions on private property without written consent. State fish and wildlife agencies gain authority and federal funding covering 75-90% of program costs. Local governments and tribes gain a seat at the table for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Landowners, developers, and state wildlife agencies

how_it_helps.text: Cooperative management agreements could be signed with local governments, Indian tribes, and private parties — not just states — and could cover species that are merely candidates for listing, before regulation starts.
Preparing, approving, and entering into an agreement would be exempt from National Environmental Policy Act review, removing one layer of environmental study.

A 'no surprises' clause bars requiring any party to an agreement to make additional payments, accept additional land restrictions, or undertake extra mitigation measures beyond what the agreement sets.
Sections 5, 7, and 9 of the Endangered Species Act — covering land acquisition, federal consultation, and prohibited takings — would not apply to activities conducted under an agreement.

The Secretary could delegate species management to states with adequate conservation programs and cover up to 75% of program costs, rising to 90% for multi-state agreements, plus financial assistance for monitoring and conservation.

analysis.who_pays: Species and their habitats would bear the main risk: agreements are insulated from environmental review and from the ESA's core protections, and their terms cannot be tightened later even as conditions change. Federal taxpayers would fund up to 90% of delegated state programs. The public loses some assurance that federal standards — and public environmental review — govern decisions about imperiled wildlife.

drawbacks.text: Exempting agreements from NEPA means no environmental assessment of the deals that decide how habitat is managed.
The 'no surprises' and provisions exempting agreement activities from ESA sections 5, 7, and 9 lock in terms that cannot be changed later, even if a species declines further.

Delegation rests on the Secretary's judgment that a state program is 'adequate,' a flexible standard; a state could gain control over species in its borders with the federal role reduced to periodic five-year review.

Supporters would counter that voluntary, consent-based agreements and federal cost-share funding can draw landowners into conservation who otherwise avoid habitat that triggers regulation; the bill does require public notice, comment, and hearings on proposed agreements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Cooperative, voluntary conservation agreements are a real and widely used tool, and paying states to do the work is not inherently bad. But this bill goes further: it wraps every agreement in exemptions from environmental review and from the ESA's most basic protections, with terms that cannot be revised as conditions change. The conservation gains of cooperation would rest on the Secretary policing each deal, with rollback available only after a party already failed to comply.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its wildlife subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young (R-AK) introduced the LAMP Act on September 24, 2019; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On October 2, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water, Oceans, and Wildlife — the last action of any kind on the bill.
The bill attracted 8 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the Endangered Species Act's existing cooperative agreement and state-cooperation provisions were left unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wildlife and habitat conservation under the current Endangered Species Act stayed intact, and the exemptions from environmental review and ESA protections were never enacted. Landowners and developers seeking relief from ESA restrictions gained nothing from this attempt.

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the Endangered Species Act
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Water, Oceans, and Wildlife subcommittee, where it received no hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were Republicans; the bill drew no Democratic cosponsors and was never advanced by the Democratic-run Natural Resources Committee.

industries.note: The bill would bar any new restriction on private property under an agreement without the owner's written consent, add a 'no surprises' guarantee against future payments or mitigation, and shield agreement activities from the ESA's takings prohibitions — reducing the cost of development on land that matters to imperiled species.

industries.industry: Agriculture, timber, mining, and energy interests operating on listed-species habitat
industries.note: Exempting agreements from NEPA review and from ESA sections 5, 7, and 9 removes environmental review and federal consultation from land and water management decisions, easing constraints on resource use.

Delegation would make states the permanent managers of endangered species within their borders, with federal funding covering 75-90% of program costs — a durable new role and revenue stream, subject only to periodic five-year review.
For the first time they could be parties to cooperative management agreements, giving communities a direct role in managing species and habitat near them.
